section.title: In the Lord I Take Refuge
section.sectionRationale: A short psalm of confidence answering the counsel to flee, in which David refuses to run from danger because the LORD is enthroned and watching, testing both righteous and wicked, and promising that the upright will see His face.
section.thesis: When counseled to flee like a bird because the foundations are being destroyed, David refuses, because the LORD is on His heavenly throne, testing every heart, and the upright, not the wicked, will ultimately see His face.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the counsel to flee and its rejection (vv1-3), the LORD's heavenly throne and His testing of all people (vv4-5), and the coming judgment on the wicked contrasted with the upright who see His face (vv6-7).

verses.text: In the LORD I {{chasah|take refuge}}. How then can you say to me: "Flee like a bird to your mountain!
For behold, the wicked bend their bows. They set their arrow on the string to shoot from the shadows at the upright in heart.
If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?"

units.label: The LORD is on His throne

verses.text: The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD is on His heavenly throne. His eyes are watching closely; they examine the sons of men.
The LORD tests the righteous and the wicked; His soul hates the lover of violence.

units.label: The upright will see His face
units.note: coals and sulfur for the wicked

verses.text: On the wicked He will rain down fiery coals and sulfur; a scorching wind will be their portion.
For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice. The upright will see His face.

chasah.gloss: To take refuge, to seek shelter, a favorite Psalter verb pictured as a bird or animal fleeing to a rock or covering for protection. David's declaration, in the LORD I take refuge, is the settled conviction that answers and refuses the counsel to flee elsewhere.

basic.context: Psalm 11 answers a specific, urgent counsel: with the wicked shooting arrows from the shadows and society's very foundations seeming to crumble, someone advises David to flee like a bird to the mountains. David refuses, because the LORD is enthroned in His holy temple, testing every heart, and the upright, not the wicked, will finally see His face.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a psalm of confidence responding to a real crisis, not a denial that danger exists; David does not pretend the arrows or the crumbling foundations are imaginary, but answers the fear of collapse with the settled fact of God's unshaken, watching throne.
basic.originalLanguages: David's opening declaration, ba'YHWH chasiti, in the LORD I take refuge, uses chasah, a verb pictured elsewhere as a bird sheltering under wings, directly answering the counsel to flee like a bird elsewhere. God's eyes 'examine,' bachan, the same verb used for testing metal in a furnace, a refining scrutiny applied to both righteous and wicked.
basic.typology: David's refusal to flee, resting instead in God's watching, testing throne, anticipates Christ, who did not flee His own hour of trial but trusted His Father's sovereign oversight completely, even to the cross.
basic.christ: Jesus refused the temptation to escape His appointed suffering, trusting the Father's sovereign throne exactly as David does here, and He is Himself the upright one who, though tested by fire, now sees the Father's face and secures that same sight for everyone united to Him.
basic.god: God is pictured here as both intimately near, in His holy temple, and cosmically sovereign, on His heavenly throne, watching every person closely with a testing gaze that examines hearts, hating violence yet loving justice and welcoming the upright to see His face.
basic.crossReferences: Habakkuk 2:20 echoes the LORD in His holy temple before whom all the earth should be silent. Hebrews 12:27-28 speaks of an unshakable kingdom amid the shaking of all else. Matthew 5:8 promises that the pure in heart will see God.
basic.oneStory: Psalm 11 answers every fear that the foundations are collapsing with the settled fact that God's throne never shakes; He watches, tests, and will finally welcome the upright to see His face, a hope secured completely in Jesus Christ, who did not flee but trusted the Father's throne through His own trial by fire.

context.literary:
Psalm 11 is a short poem built like a small courtroom drama in two panels. The first panel, verses 1 to 3, belongs to the crowd. The psalmist quotes his frightened friends: 'Flee like a bird to your mountain,' and gives their three reasons, the bent bows, the arrows in the dark, and the crumbling foundations. Their speech ends in a question with no answer, 'what can the righteous do?' The second panel, verses 4 to 7, is the psalmist's reply, and it is not a rebuttal of their facts but a change of place. He moves the reader from the ground where arrows fly to the throne room where they are counted.

The two panels are matched with care. The friends speak of a 'mountain' to flee to; the psalmist speaks of a 'temple' and a 'throne' in heaven. They speak of the wicked who 'shoot' at the 'upright'; he speaks of the LORD who 'tests' the righteous and rains fire on the wicked. They speak of foundations destroyed; he ends on a righteous God. The verb of seeing carries the design. In verse 4 the LORD's eyes 'watch closely,' and in verse 7 the upright 'will see His face,' so the poem is a movement from being watched to seeing.

The psalm runs from anxiety to certainty in seven verses and does it without narrating any change in circumstances. The arrows are still on the string at the end. What has changed is the vantage point. There is also a quiet reversal in verse 6. The wicked who shoot rain-like arrows from the shadows are themselves to receive a rain, of fire and sulfur, from above. Those who ambush in the dark are seen in the light.
context.historical:
The psalm is headed as David's in the Hebrew, and its likeliest backdrop is the years when Saul hunted him. A counsellor's advice to 'flee like a bird to your mountain' fits a man who did spend his days in the wilderness of Judah and was told to keep running. David could say later to Saul that the king of Israel had come out to hunt 'a partridge in the mountains,' 1 Samuel 26:20, and the image of a small bird on a hill was one David had lived. The psalm does not tie itself to any one episode, and that lets it be sung whenever an honest man is told his cause is lost.

The sanctuary language deserves a note. 'His holy temple,' verse 4, uses a word that could be applied to a shrine such as Shiloh, where Eli sat by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD, 1 Samuel 1:9, and it does not require Solomon's building. David knew a tent for the ark. The psalm's claim is that the earthly place of meeting is the shadow of the throne in heaven, a link Israel's worship made in every generation, 1 Kings 8:30.

The bows and arrows of verse 2 were the weapon of ambush in the hill country, and 'from the shadows' means literally in darkness, the setting of the assassin. The 'foundations' of verse 3 are the pillars of social order, the courts, the covenant, the ordinary trust between neighbours, which Israel knew could be undermined by lawless power, as Psalm 82:5 mourns.

Fire and sulfur were the signature of Sodom's fall, Genesis 19:24, and the first hearers would hear in verse 6 an allusion to that story. In a culture where an honest court was the shield of the poor, the threat that God would rain judgment on those who corrupt justice was a reminder that the highest court was not corrupt.
context.canonical:
Psalm 11 begins the run of short psalms in Book One that answer fear with a fact about God. Its central claim, that the LORD is on His throne, is the Psalter's constant refrain: Psalm 2:4 'The One enthroned in heaven laughs,' Psalm 93:1 'The LORD reigns,' Psalm 103:19. The image of God's eyes examining humanity has a companion in Psalm 33:13 to 15, where He looks down from heaven and considers all their works. The verb of testing hearts appears again in Psalm 7:9, 'O righteous God who searches hearts and minds,' and Psalm 26:2, 'Test me, O LORD, and try me.' What the righteous person asks for in Psalm 26 is what God does to every person in Psalm 11.

The chapter's word about fire and sulfur travels through Scripture as the emblem of final judgment. Ezekiel 38:22 pours it on Gog's armies, Luke 17:29 recalls Sodom, and Revelation 21:8 names the lake that burns with fire and sulfur as the second death. The psalm's cup imagery, 'the portion of their cup,' belongs to the cup of wrath of Psalm 75:8, and to the cup that Jesus asks to be taken from Him, Matthew 26:39.

The hope of verse 7, that the upright will see His face, is one of the great desires of the Psalter, Psalm 17:15, 27:4 and 42:2. Jesus takes it up in the Beatitudes, 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God,' Matthew 5:8, and John promises that 'we will see Him as He is,' 1 John 3:2. It closes the Bible: 'They will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. Hebrews, speaking of the shaking of heaven and earth, describes 'an unshakable kingdom,' Hebrews 12:28, which is the reply the whole canon makes to the question 'If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David meant to teach the faithful how to answer well meant despair. The advice in verses 1 to 3 is not wicked. It is the sensible counsel of people who love him, and it rests on true facts. That is exactly why it is dangerous. The psalm shows that prudence built only on visible facts can lead the righteous to abandon their post. David's answer is to bring one more fact into the calculation, and it outweighs the others: 'The LORD is on His heavenly throne.'

He also meant to teach that trust in God is not the same as a lack of danger. The psalmist never denies the bows. He does not say the wicked are weak. The psalm holds the danger and the throne in the same frame and lets the throne decide. That is the lesson for anyone facing threats: faith takes the dangers seriously and takes God more seriously.

There is also a stern instruction in the psalm about the character of God's watching. The same eyes that shelter the upright examine everyone, and the psalm does not let the reader think of God's attention as a merely comforting fact. Verses 5 and 6 are meant to be heard by those who use power for violence, and the psalm holds a warning within the comfort.

Finally, the closing promise is meant to set the hearers' eyes on a reward that lies beyond safety. The upright are not promised that the arrows will miss. They are promised that they will see His face. It is a promise that turns the aim of the believer from being spared to being with God, and it fits the whole design of the psalm, which moves from fear to sight.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes David's decision to stay and trust; it does not lay down a rule that the faithful may never flee. Scripture elsewhere records wise and godly flight. David himself ran from Saul's spear, 1 Samuel 19:10, Joseph took the child to Egypt, Matthew 2:13, and Jesus told His disciples, 'When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next,' Matthew 10:23. So Psalm 11 cannot be turned into an argument against prudence, escape or self defence.

What the psalm asks for is a different thing: that the decision, whether to flee or to stay, be made from confidence in God and not from panic about the foundations. The counsel in verse 1 fails not because running is wrong but because it is offered as a rescue from a world in which God has abdicated. The psalmist's refusal is a refusal of that premise.

The descriptions of judgment in verse 6 are also not commissions. The fire and sulfur are God's to send. Believers are not told to rain anything down on their enemies. They are told, by the design of the psalm, to hold the fear of the wicked and the fact of the throne together, and to leave the coals to the one who sits there. The promise of verse 7 is a hope, not a demand, and it is a hope of the upright, which means that those who read it are directed to uprightness rather than to certainty about who is next.

debates.question: Who is speaking the counsel to flee in verses 1-3, David's own advisors or the wicked themselves?

views.label: Well-meaning advisors urging a pragmatic retreat
views.case: The counsel reads as sober, practical advice from people around David who see real danger, arrows from the shadows, and reasonably suggest flight as the wise course.

views.label: A taunt from the wicked designed to provoke fear and abandonment of trust
views.case: Given the psalm's contrast between the wicked's violence and David's refuge in God, some read the counsel to flee as coming from, or echoing, the very enemies described, intended to shake David's confidence.

debates.bearing: Either way, David's response is the same and instructive: he answers the counsel to flee, whatever its source, not by denying real danger but by anchoring his confidence in God's unshaken throne rather than in escape.

debates.question: Where is the 'holy temple' of verse 4?

views.label: The earthly sanctuary in Jerusalem or its predecessor
views.case: The Hebrew word can name the sanctuary building, and David's world had a tabernacle and, in the Psalter's later life, a temple. On this reading verse 4 sets the earthly place of worship, where the LORD is present to His people, beside His heavenly rule, and the psalmist draws confidence from the place where God has promised to meet Israel.

views.label: The heavenly temple, identical with the throne
views.case: The second half of the verse, 'the LORD is on His heavenly throne,' is parallel to the first, so many take 'temple' as the heavenly palace, God's true dwelling. Isaiah saw the LORD on a throne with the train of His robe filling the temple, Isaiah 6:1, and Hebrews describes a true tabernacle set up by the Lord, Hebrews 8:1 and 2.

views.label: Both, as one reality seen from two sides
views.case: Israel's worship treated the sanctuary as a copy or a doorway of the heavenly court, so that the psalm can speak of the temple and the throne without choosing. Solomon prays that God will hear from heaven when His people pray toward the house, 1 Kings 8:30.

debates.bearing: The three readings agree on what matters for the psalm's argument, that God is neither absent from the world nor overwhelmed by it. The temple speaks of His nearness and the throne of His rule, and the psalmist rests on both.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm's structure hangs on the Hebrew verb chazah, 'to see, to gaze,' the verb of visions and of looking intently. In verse 4 the LORD's eyes 'watch closely,' and in verse 7 the upright 'will see His face,' and both use chazah. The poem opens with a God who looks and ends with people who look back. The same verse 4 contains a striking detail the English loses: the Hebrew says His 'eyelids' test the sons of men. The picture is of a person narrowing his eyes to study something closely, and it makes the divine attention intimate and intent, not a passing glance.

The word 'foundations' in verse 3 is yesodot, the underpinnings of a building, and by extension the settled order of a society. Psalm 82:5 uses the related idea when 'all the foundations of the earth are shaken' by unjust judges. The question 'what can the righteous do?' asks what one person can achieve when the structure holding everything up has been undermined. The Hebrew does not say the foundations are being destroyed by nature; the setting suggests it is the work of the men who bend their bows.

The 'upright in heart' of verse 2 is a phrase found in the Psalter of those who are honest before God, as in Psalm 7:10 and 32:11. It is the psalmist's own class. The target of the arrows is those whose only fault is that their hearts are straight.

Verse 5 says 'His soul hates,' using nefesh, the word for the whole living self. This is not an outburst of temper but a verdict of God's whole being against violence. The same Hebrew attitude is voiced in Psalm 5:5, 'You hate all workers of iniquity,' and Hebrews 1:9 applies to the Son 'You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness.'

Verse 6 has the words 'fire and sulfur,' the pair that describes the destruction of Sodom in Genesis 19:24, and the Hebrew for sulfur is gofrit. The phrase 'their portion' is literally 'the portion of their cup,' a metaphor of a measured allotment poured out by God, as in Psalm 75:8. The psalm reverses the cup of blessing in Psalm 16:5 and 23:5. The wicked receive a cup too, but of a different kind.

The last verse contains a matter of grammar. The Hebrew says 'the upright will see His face,' but the verb is plural and 'face' is a plural noun form, and the word for 'upright' is a singular that can act as a collective. A few interpreters read it as 'His face beholds the upright,' which would return the psalm's opening image of a watching God. The BSB reads the more natural sense, that the upright see. The claim of this verse is that righteousness is not only what God loves in verse 7, tsedaqot in the Hebrew, 'righteous acts,' but also what God rewards, so that the psalm ends where the psalm's hope lies, in the vision of God.

typology.fulfillment: David answers those who tell him to run by staying. Jesus is the fuller pattern. Luke says 'He resolutely set out for Jerusalem,' Luke 9:51, and in the garden, John records that Jesus, 'knowing all that was coming upon Him, stepped forward,' John 18:4, and when they came for Him He asked whom they were seeking. He had said earlier that He would not ask the Father to save Him from this hour, John 12:27. The type falls short in one way: David's stand was a defensive one, while Jesus went towards the danger for the sake of others. The pattern is not that a believer should never withdraw, since Jesus did at other times, Matthew 12:15.

typology.type: The portion of the wicked's cup, Psalm 11:6
typology.fulfillment: The psalm speaks of a cup of judgment that the wicked must drink. The Gospels present Jesus taking that cup on behalf of others. In Gethsemane He prays, 'Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. The link is an inference from the shared image of a cup, and the Gospels do not quote Psalm 11. But Isaiah 51:17 and Psalm 75:8 make the cup an image of God's wrath, and the New Testament teaches that Christ bore it in our place, Romans 3:25. The correspondence is real but the pattern reverses: in the psalm the wicked drink; at the cross the righteous one drinks.

typology.type: The foundations that cannot be shaken, Psalm 11:3
typology.fulfillment: The psalm asks what the righteous can do when the foundations are gone. The New Testament answers with a person. Isaiah spoke of a tested stone, a precious cornerstone and a sure foundation, and said 'the one who believes will never be shaken,' Isaiah 28:16. Paul says the household of God is built on the apostles and prophets 'with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone,' Ephesians 2:20, and Jesus says the man who hears His words and acts on them is like one who built on the rock, Matthew 7:24 and 25. The correspondence is real, but the psalm's foundations were social order, and the fulfilment adds a kingdom that cannot be shaken, Hebrews 12:28.

typology.type: The upright who will see His face, Psalm 11:7
typology.fulfillment: The psalm ends with the promise that the upright will see the LORD's face. In Christ that hope is met. Stephen, dying, looked into heaven and saw 'the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God,' Acts 7:55. Jesus Himself is the upright one, who in Hebrews is the one who 'loved righteousness and hated wickedness,' Hebrews 1:9, and John says that when Christ appears 'we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is,' 1 John 3:2. The type reaches its end in Revelation 22:4, 'They will see His face.' The pattern is incomplete now, since believers see by faith and not yet by sight.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the pattern of the one who does not run. The counsel of verse 1 is a temptation to abandon the post because the foundations are shaking, and Jesus faced the same pressure at greater cost. His own family and friends urged caution, Peter rebuked Him for speaking of the cross, and in the garden His soul was 'consumed with sorrow to the point of death,' Mark 14:34. Yet He fell to the ground and prayed, and then stepped forward to meet those who came to seize Him, John 18:4. David's 'In the LORD I take refuge' is in Christ's mouth a full surrender, 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' Luke 23:46. The one who trusted the throne while the arrows flew was the one who had the most to lose.

It leads to Christ by the figure of the upright one. In the psalm the 'upright in heart' are the target of the arrows and the object of God's love. The New Testament says of Jesus that 'no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22, and applies to Him the words 'You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness,' Hebrews 1:9, which are the very attitudes verse 7 attributes to the LORD. The Son who mirrors the Father's love of justice is also the one whom the wicked shot at and killed. Yet God tested Him and found Him faithful, and the throne received Him. He is the upright one who has seen the Father's face and who opens that sight to others.

It leads to Christ in judgment. The fire and sulfur of verse 6 are, in the New Testament, the fate of those who refuse Him, Revelation 21:8, and the Son is the appointed judge, Acts 17:31. The psalm is not embarrassed by judgment and neither is the gospel. The tenderness of Christ does not mean the end of justice, and this is stated by the one who spoke most about the lake of fire.

It leads to Christ by the promise of sight. 'The upright will see His face.' Jesus is the face of God, 'the exact representation of His nature,' Hebrews 1:3, and He says 'Whoever has seen Me has seen the Father,' John 14:9. To see Him now by faith is the beginning of that sight, and to see Him as He is, 1 John 3:2, is its completion.

A note of caution keeps the reading honest. The psalm does not mention a Messiah, and its enemies are David's own. Not every detail, the bird, the mountain, the eyelids, is a picture of Jesus. The connections rest on what the New Testament itself does with these themes, the throne, the testing, the cup, the face, and on the pattern of the upright sufferer that runs through the Psalter and finds its fulfilment in one man.
study.god:
Psalm 11 shows God in His temple and on His throne at once, and it presents these as one truth seen from two sides. The temple is where He meets His people, and the heavenly throne is where He rules the world. The psalm does not choose between nearness and sovereignty. Isaiah 66:1 says heaven is His throne and earth His footstool, and Psalm 11 lives in that space.

God sees, and His seeing is judgment. This is the doctrine of divine omniscience without abstraction. It is not merely that God knows facts but that He is looking at people, closely, with narrowed eyes. The two halves of verse 5 show that this attention falls on the righteous and the wicked both. Jeremiah 17:10 says the LORD searches the heart and examines the mind to give each what their deeds deserve. The psalm removes any suggestion that God's watchfulness is only a comfort. It is also the reason no one hides.

He is a God who hates and a God who loves, and the psalm lets both stand. 'His soul hates the lover of violence,' verse 5, and 'He loves justice,' verse 7. Some pictures of God prefer only the second. The psalm insists that love of the good has an edge, that a God who loved the poor and did not hate their oppressor would be less than good. His hatred is not the lashing out of a wounded ego; it is the opposite side of His righteousness.

He is the God who acts, though on His own timing. The fire and sulfur belong to a future action, and the psalm does not say when. He is patient without being passive. The psalm asks the reader to trust a God whose governance does not need to be visible each hour to be real.

He tests. The word for the testing of the righteous suggests refining, and the psalm places the testing of the righteous next to the judgment of the wicked. God is doing something with the righteous while the arrows fly, and it is not abandonment. Zechariah 13:9 speaks of refining people like silver and gold, and 1 Peter 4:12 tells believers not to be surprised at the fiery trial.

For worship, the psalm teaches where to look. The believer's first act in crisis is to fix on the throne, not on the foundations, which means worship is not an escape from reality but the truest description of it. The God who is worshipped in the temple is the one who sits on the throne, and those who come to Him in worship are those who will see His face. The psalm keeps the terror and the beauty together, and it teaches that they are not two gods but one.

crossReferences.note: David asks the righteous God who searches hearts and minds to put an end to the evil of the wicked and establish the righteous. It describes the same activity as Psalm 11:4 and 5, the LORD examining people from within, and it shows the testing as a source of confidence for the innocent.

David tells Saul that the king has come out to hunt a partridge in the mountains. It gives the likely biography behind Psalm 11:1, the counsel to flee like a bird to the mountain, and shows that David knew what it meant to be hunted on the hills and still declared he took refuge in the LORD.

Unjust judges leave the foundations of the earth shaken. It places Psalm 11:3 in a wider setting, where the foundations are the order of justice and not merely the soil. When courts turn against the righteous, the structure that holds a society up begins to fall.

The LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah. This is the great precedent for Psalm 11:6. The psalm reminds readers that fire from heaven is not a legend but a memory of God acting against a city that gave itself to violence.

After the prophet has protested at length against violence, God's reply is a call to hush, because He is present in His sanctuary. The line matches the opening of Psalm 11:4, and the prophet uses it the same way, to move a troubled heart from the spectacle of wrong to the fact of the throne.

A cup in the LORD's hand is full of foaming wine, and all the wicked of the earth drink it to the dregs. It explains the image behind the 'portion' of Psalm 11:6 and shows that the cup of judgment is a settled theme of the Psalter.

The wise man builds on rock, and the rain and winds do not topple the house. Jesus answers the question of Psalm 11:3 by telling His hearers what a secure foundation is, hearing His words and doing them. The answer to shaken foundations is to build elsewhere.

The writer speaks of the removal of what can be shaken so that the unshakable may remain, and says believers are receiving an unshakable kingdom. It is the New Testament answer to the psalm's fear, that when everything shakes there is a kingdom that stays.

David says he will behold God's face in righteousness and be satisfied on awaking. It shares the hope of Psalm 11:7 and gives it the horizon of resurrection, so that seeing His face is the final satisfaction and not merely a present comfort.

They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads. It is the last word of the Bible on the promise of Psalm 11:7. The hope of the upright is fulfilled in the new creation, where the face once seen by faith is seen openly.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 11 belongs to the long story of a world in which the foundations really do seem to shift. It looks back to the garden, where humanity hid from God's presence and were sent away from it, Genesis 3:8 and 24. The whole history of human life since then has been lived under the shadow of that loss of sight. The psalm's hope, that the upright will see His face, is the reversal of that expulsion. What was lost at the beginning is what the psalm says will be given back.

It looks back also to a violent world. Cain's sin was the first arrow in the dark, and by the time of the flood 'the earth was filled with violence,' Genesis 6:11. God's response there was a judgment that fell from above, and His response to Sodom was fire and sulfur, Genesis 19:24. Psalm 11 stands in that tradition of a God who sees violence and does not let it stand.

The story moves forward through the exile, when the foundations of Israel, the temple, the throne and the land, were in fact destroyed, and people had to ask the psalm's question in earnest. The prophets answered that the LORD was still in His temple, Habakkuk 2:20, and that He would lay a new foundation, a tested stone in Zion, Isaiah 28:16.

Christ is that stone, and He is the upright one who was shot at in the dark by those who arrested Him at night and was tested by the Father. He did not flee and was raised. He is the shelter into which His people run, not to escape the world but to be kept in it. And the story moves to its end in an unshakable kingdom, Hebrews 12:28, where fire and sulfur belong to the enemies of God, Revelation 21:8, and the upright are given what the psalm promised. The tree of life is restored, the curse is gone, and 'they will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. The exile from the garden is finally over, and the question 'what can the righteous do?' has its answer: they can trust, and they will see.

sermon.title: Runaway World
sermon.why: Begg preaches through Psalm 11:1-7, urging believers to learn from the tumultuous life of King David that we will only endure life's difficulties and Satan's snares if God is our refuge, rather than running from our troubles.

quiz.q: What counsel does David receive at the start of Psalm 11?

options.text: To flee like a bird to the mountains, since the wicked are shooting arrows and the foundations are being destroyed.
options.note: This is the specific counsel of despair the psalm opens by quoting.

options.text: To attack his enemies directly.
options.note: The counsel given is to flee, not to attack; David's response is neither fleeing nor attacking but taking refuge in God.

options.text: To offer a sacrifice for forgiveness.
options.note: No sacrifice is mentioned; the counsel specifically urges flight from danger.

options.text: To seek an alliance with a foreign king.
options.note: This is not the counsel described; the specific advice given is to flee to the mountains.

quiz.q: How does David respond to this counsel?

options.text: He declares that he takes refuge in the LORD rather than fleeing.
options.note: This is David's opening declaration and settled response to the counsel to flee.

options.text: He immediately flees as advised.
options.note: David explicitly rejects this counsel, declaring his refuge is in the LORD instead.

options.text: He ignores the danger entirely.
options.note: David does not deny the danger is real; he answers it with trust in God rather than denial or flight.

options.text: He gives no response at all.
options.note: Verse 1 is a direct, explicit response rejecting the counsel to flee.

quiz.q: What does the LORD do, according to verses 4-5?

options.text: He sits enthroned in His holy temple and heavenly throne, His eyes watching closely and testing both the righteous and the wicked.
options.note: This describes God's sovereign, attentive oversight of all humanity.

options.text: He is absent from His temple during times of crisis.
options.note: The text explicitly affirms God's presence and active watching, not absence.

options.text: He tests only the wicked, never the righteous.
options.note: Verse 5 explicitly says the LORD tests both the righteous and the wicked.

options.text: He has no interest in human affairs.
options.note: The text describes God's eyes closely watching and examining, the opposite of disinterest.

quiz.q: What is promised to the wicked in verse 6?

options.text: The LORD will rain down fiery coals and sulfur on them, and a scorching wind will be their portion.
options.note: This vivid image of judgment describes the wicked's coming fate.

options.text: They will prosper permanently with no consequence.
options.note: The text explicitly describes coming judgment, not permanent prosperity.

options.text: They will be given a final chance to repent with no judgment described.
options.note: Verse 6 describes specific judgment, not merely an offer of repentance.

options.text: Nothing; the psalm makes no mention of judgment for the wicked.
options.note: Verse 6 explicitly describes coming judgment on the wicked.

quiz.q: What is promised to the upright in verse 7?

options.text: They will see His face, because the LORD is righteous and loves justice.
options.note: This is the psalm's closing promise for the upright, contrasted with the wicked's judgment.

options.text: They will receive great material wealth.
options.note: The promise given is specifically to see God's face, not a promise of material wealth.

options.text: They will never face any hardship again.
options.note: The promise is relational and future, seeing God's face, not a guarantee against present hardship.

options.text: Nothing is promised to the upright.
options.note: Verse 7 explicitly promises the upright will see His face.

questions: David is counseled to flee from danger, but instead declares his refuge is in the LORD. When you face pressure to run from a hard situation, what would it look like for you to take refuge in God instead of simply escaping?

David does not deny that real arrows are being shot and real foundations are shaking; he answers real danger with real trust. Where in your life do you need to hold both truths together, honest acknowledgment of danger and confident trust in God?
The LORD's eyes examine and test both the righteous and the wicked, like a refiner testing metal. What is God currently testing or refining in your own heart through your present circumstances?

The psalm contrasts the coming judgment of the wicked with the promise that the upright will see God's face. How does the hope of one day seeing God face to face shape the way you endure present difficulty?

Jesus refused every opportunity to escape His appointed suffering, trusting His Father's sovereign throne completely. How does His example strengthen you to stay faithful in a situation you are currently tempted to flee?

translationNotes.note: Flee like a bird to your mountain pictures a bird escaping to a rocky crag for safety, a common image for retreat to a place of natural refuge, here contrasted with David's chosen refuge in the LORD Himself.

His eyes are watching closely, they examine renders a Hebrew verb, bachan, elsewhere used for testing or refining metal by fire, describing God's scrutiny as a discerning, purifying examination rather than mere observation.

The upright will see His face is among the earliest scriptural expressions of the hope, developed more fully later in Scripture, of direct, unmediated fellowship with God as the believer's final reward, echoed in Matthew 5:8 and Revelation 22:4.
